n: *Study note:* Ezek 21:1 in the English Bible is 21:6 in the Hebrew text (*BHS*). See the note at 20:45.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the land of Israel.”

*Translator's note:* The word הִנֵּה (hinneh, traditionally “behold”) draws attention to something and has been translated here as a verb.

*Translator's note:* Or “I challenge you.” The phrase “I am against you” may be a formula for challenging someone to combat or a duel. See D. I. Block, *Ezekiel* (NICOT), 1:201-2, and P. Humbert, “Die Herausforderungsformel ‘hinnenî ’êlékâ’” *ZAW 45* (1933): 101-8.

*Study note:* This is the sword of judgment; see {{Isaiah 31:8|Isa 31:8}}; {{Isaiah 34:6|34:6}}; {{Isaiah 66:16|66:16}}.

*Study note:* Ezekiel elsewhere pictures the Lord’s judgment as discriminating between the righteous and the wicked ({{Ezekiel 9:4|9:4-6}}; {{Ezekiel 18:1|18:1-20}}; see as well {{Psalm 1|Pss 1}} and {{Psalm 11|11}}) and speaks of the preservation of a remnant ({{Ezekiel 3:21|3:21}}; {{Ezekiel 6:8|6:8}}; {{Ezekiel 12:16|12:16}}). Perhaps here he exaggerates for rhetorical effect in an effort to subdue any false optimism. See L. C. Allen, *Ezekiel* (WBC), 2:25-26; D. I. Block, *Ezekiel* (NICOT), 1:669-70; and W. Zimmerli, *Ezekiel* (Hermeneia), 1:424-25. The words do not require all the people in each category to be cut off.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “all flesh” (also in the following verse).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “Negev.” The Negev is the south country.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “every spirit will be dim.”

*Study note:* This expression depicts in a very vivid way how they will be overcome with fear. See the note on the same phrase in {{Ezekiel 7:17|7:17}}.

*Study note:* The people of Judah should not place false hope in their king, symbolized by his royal scepter, for God’s judgment (symbolized by fire and then a sword) would destroy every tree (see {{Ezekiel 20:47|20:47}}), symbolizing the righteous and wicked (see {{Ezekiel 21:3|21:3-4}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “Or shall we rejoice, scepter of my son? It despises every tree.” The translation understands the subject of the verb “despises,” which is a feminine form in the Hebrew text, to be the sword (which is a feminine noun) mentioned just before this. Alternatively, the line may be understood as “Let us not rejoice, O tribe of my son; it despises every tree.” The same word in Hebrew may be either “rod,” “scepter,” or “tribe.” The word sometimes translated as “or” or taken as an interrogative particle may be a negative particle. See D. I. Block, *Ezekiel* (NICOT), 1:672, n. 79.
*Study note:* This physical action was part of an expression of grief. Cf. Jer 31:19.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “For testing (will come), and what if also a scepter it despises will not be?” The translation understands the subject of the verb “despises,” which is a feminine form in the Hebrew text, to be the sword (which is a feminine noun) mentioned in the previous verses. The text is very difficult, and any rendering is uncertain.

*Text-critical note:* The MT reads “Judah in fortified Jerusalem,” a geographic impossibility. The translation follows the LXX, which assumes בְּתוֹכָהּ (betokhah, “in it”) for בְּצוּרָה (betsurah, “fortified”).

*Study note:* As the Babylonians approached from the north, one road would branch off to the left and lead down the east side of the Jordan River to Ammon. The other road would veer to the right and lead down west of the Jordan to Jerusalem.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “mother.”

*Study note:* Mesopotamian kings believed that the gods revealed the future through omens. They employed various divination techniques, some of which are included in the list that follows. A particularly popular technique was the examination and interpretation of the livers of animals. See R. R. Wilson, *Prophecy and Society in Ancient Israel*, 90-110.

*Translator's note:* This word refers to personal idols that were apparently used for divination purposes ({{Genesis 31:19|Gen 31:19}}; {{1 Samuel 19:13|1 Sam 19:13}}, {{1 Samuel 19:16|16}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “sees.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the liver.”

*Translator's note:* Or “on the right side,” i.e., the omen mark on the right side of the liver.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “to open the mouth” for slaughter.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “to raise up a voice in a battle cry.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “they”; the referent (the people in Jerusalem) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

*Study note:* When the people of Judah realized the Babylonians’ intentions, they would object on grounds that they had made a treaty with the Babylonian king (see {{Ezekiel 17:13|17:13}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “he”; the referent (the king of Babylon) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

*Translator's note:* Or “iniquity.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and he will remind of guilt to be captured.” The king would counter their objections by pointing out that they had violated their treaty with him (see {{Ezekiel 17:18|17:18}}), thus justifying their capture.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “caused to be remembered.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “Because you have brought to remembrance your guilt when your transgressions are uncovered so that your sins are revealed in all your deeds—because you are remembered, by the hand you will be seized.”
*Translator's note:* This probably refers to King Zedekiah.

*Translator's note:* Elsewhere in the Bible the turban is worn by priests ({{Exodus 28:4|Exod 28:4}}, {{Exodus 28:37|37}}, {{Exodus 28:39|39}}; {{Exodus 29:6|29:6}}; {{Exodus 39:28|39:28}}, {{Exodus 39:31|31}}; Lev 8:9; 16:4), but here a royal crown is in view.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “This not this.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the high one.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “A ruin, a ruin, a ruin I will make it.” The threefold repetition of the noun “ruin” is for emphasis and draws attention to the degree of ruin that would take place. See *IBHS* 233 §12.5a and GKC 431-32 §133.*k*. The pronominal suffix (translated “it”) on the verb “make” is feminine in Hebrew. The probable antecedent is the “turban/crown” (both nouns are feminine in form) mentioned in verse {{Ezekiel 21:26|26}}. The point is that the king’s royal splendor would be completely devastated as judgment overtook his realm and brought his reign to a violent end.

*Translator's note:* The pronoun “this” is feminine, while the following negated verb (“will not be”) is masculine. Some emend the verb to a feminine form (see *BHS*), In this case the statement refers to the destiny of the king's turban crown (symbolizing his reign). See the previous note. It ultimately denotes kingship in Israel, as with “not this” in v. {{Ezekiel 21:26|26}}.

*Translator's note:* Horace D. Hummel, *Ezekiel* (Concordia Commentary), 2:642, states that the suffixed object of the Hebrew verb for “give” (נָתַן, natan) can be indirect: “to him,” while the direct object (“it”) is understood from the preceding “right.” However, a more likely candidate for the understood object would be “this,” the turban/crown and the kingship it implies. The one who comes already has the “right.”

*Study note:* A popular alternative view of this verse takes “right” as “judgment,” views the one who comes as Nebuchadnezzar, and translates “until” (עַד, ‘ad) as “when.” The basis for this unique translation of עַד (which rarely can mean “while”) is that here it would refer to the period during which the devastation is realized rather than to its termination point. See L. C. Allen, *Ezekiel* (WBC), 2:19, 21. Ezekiel often has מִשְׁפָּט as “judgment” and does not use it elsewhere as “right.” God promises to “give” “judgment” to the Babylonians in {{Ezekiel 23:24|23:24}}, as he would here. However, “right” is a normal sense for מִשְׁפָּט, and even most who see Nebuchadnezzar as the one who comes find an allusion to {{Genesis 49:10|Gen 49:10}} here, though inverted. However, this verse can alter the idea of {{Genesis 49:10|Gen 49:10}} even without Allen’s view, since {{Genesis 49:10|Gen 49:10}} promises that the scepter will not depart from Judah until the Messiah comes, while {{Ezekiel 21:27|Ezek 21:27}} promises that the royal turban/crown will be a ruin until Messiah comes. Robert W. Jenson, *Ezekiel* (Brazos Theological Commentary on the Bible), 173, favors the traditional view “because of the eschatological rhetoric of the whole poem,” adding that “ending merely with Nebuchadnezzar would be a poetically disastrous anticlimax.” For {{Ezekiel 34:23|Ezek 34:23-24}} and {{Ezekiel 37:22|37:22}}, {{Ezekiel 37:24|24-25}} promise the restoration of Davidic kingship in the Messiah.

*Translator's note:* Hummel, *Ezekiel*, 2:658, states that “very early” interpreters saw similarity between this verse and {{Genesis 49:10|Gen 49:10}}. Early Christian scholars like Jerome interpreted {{Ezekiel 21:27|Ezek 21:27}} of Jesus Christ, as did the majority of Christian scholars until rather recent times. The phrase “until he comes to whom it belongs” in {{Genesis 49:10|Gen 49:10}} resembles the words here. “Until” and “comes” are the same in both verses. In both verses there follows a relative pronoun like “who,” the preposition “to,” a prepositional object “him,” and an understood linking verb “is.” An allusion would favor those Hebrew words having the same meaning in both verses, with “right, legal claim” as the sense for מִשְׁפָּט, (mishpat) rather than “judgment,” since it is more compatible with an allusion.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “their reproach.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “to contain, endure,” from כוּל (khul). Since that sense is difficult here, most take the text to read either “to consume” or “for destruction.” GKC 186 §68.i suggests that the form represents the Hiphil of אָכַל (’akhal, “consume”). The ’alef (א) would have dropped out, as it sometimes does and might do with אָכַל in {{Ezekiel 42:5|Ezek 42:5}}. D. I. Block (*Ezekiel* [NICOT], 1:693) prefers seeing כוּל as a byform of כָּלָה (kalah, “be complete”), with a meaning like “consume” in the Hiphil. The weakness of Block’s suggestion is that כָּלָה does not elsewhere exhibit a Hiphil.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “in the seeing concerning you falsehood, in divining concerning you a lie.” This probably refers to the attempts of the Ammonites to ward off judgment through prophetic visions and divination.

*Translator's note:* The antecedent for *you* is the sword mentioned in v. {{Ezekiel 21:28|28}}.

*Study note:* The second half of the verse appears to state that the sword of judgment would fall upon the wicked Ammonites, despite their efforts to prevent it.

*Study note:* Once the Babylonian king’s sword (vv. {{Ezekiel 21:19|19-20}}) has carried out its assigned task, the Lord commands a halt. The resheathed sword will return to the land where it was created, and there itself face judgment. The pronouns continue to be second person feminine singular. The sword figuratively represents the Babylonian nation, whose land is the locus of judgment.

*Translator's note:* In the Hebrew text of vv. {{Ezekiel 21:30|30-32}} the second person verbal and pronominal forms are generally feminine singular. This continues the address of the personified Babylonian sword from verse {{Ezekiel 21:29|29}} (the Hebrew word for “sword” is feminine). “Return” is masculine, either due to the Hebrew preference for the masculine gender, or to the fact that soldiers were men.
*Study note:* The imagery of blowing on the sword with fire and putting it in the hands of skillful men can evoke the work of smithies.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “your blood will be in the middle of the land.”

*Study note:* This can be the blood that covered the sword in its great slaughter (v. {{Ezekiel 21:14|14}}), figuratively representing the end of Babylon. The pronouns are still second person feminine singular.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “will you judge.” Here the imperfect form of the verb is probably used with a desiderative nuance. Addressed to the prophet, “judge” means to warn of or pronounce God’s impending judgment upon the city. See {{Ezekiel 20:4|20:4}}.

*Translator's note:* The phrase “bloody city” is used of Nineveh in Nah 3:1.
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “her time”; this refers to the time of impending judgment (see the note on “doom” in v. {{Ezekiel 22:4|4}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “you have brought near your days.” The expression “bring near your days” appears to be an adaptation of the idiom “days draw near,” which is used to indicate that an event, such as death, is imminent (see {{Genesis 27:41|Gen 27:41}}; {{Genesis 47:29|47:29}}; {{Deuteronomy 31:14|Deut 31:14}}; {{1 Kings 2:1|1 Kgs 2:1}}; {{Ezekiel 12:23|Ezek 12:23}}). Here “your days” probably refer to the days of the personified city’s life, which was about to come to an end through God’s judgment.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and you have come to your years.” This appears to mean that she has arrived at the time when her years (i.e., life) would end, though it may mean that her years of punishment will begin. Because “day” and “time” are so closely associated in the immediate context (see {{Ezekiel 21:25|21:25}}, {{Ezekiel 21:29|29}}), some prefer to emend the text and read: “you have brought near your time.” See L. C. Allen, *Ezekiel* (WBC), 2:31, as well as the translator’s note on verse {{Ezekiel 22:3|3}}.

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew verb is a prophetic perfect, emphasizing that the action is as good as done from the speaker’s perspective.
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “Look! The princes of Israel, each according to his arm, were in you in order to shed blood.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “treated lightly, cursed.”

*Translator's note:* Widows and orphans are often coupled together in the OT ({{Deuteronomy 14:29|Deut 14:29}}; {{Deuteronomy 16:11|16:11}}, {{Deuteronomy 16:14|14}}; {{Deuteronomy 24:19|24:19-21}}; {{Deuteronomy 26:12|26:12-13}}; Jer 7:6; 22:3). They represented all who were poor and vulnerable to economic exploitation.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “men of slander are in you in order to shed blood.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and on the mountains they eat within you.” The mountains mentioned here were the site of pagan sacrifices. See {{Ezekiel 18:6|18:6}}.

*Study note:* This statement introduces vv. {{Ezekiel 22:10|10-11}} and refers in general terms to the sexual sins described there. For the legal background of vv. {{Ezekiel 22:10|10-11}}, see Lev 18:7-20; 20:10-21; {{Deuteronomy 22:22|Deut 22:22-23}}, {{Deuteronomy 22:30|30}}; {{Deuteronomy 27:22|27:22}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “The nakedness of a father one uncovers within you.” The ancient versions read the verb as plural (“they uncover”). If the singular is retained, it must be taken as indefinite and representative of the entire group. The idiomatic expression “uncover the nakedness” refers here to sexual intercourse (cf. Lev 18:6). To uncover a father’s nakedness could include sexual relations with one’s own mother (Lev 18:7), but more likely it refers to having intercourse with another wife of one’s father, such as a stepmother (Lev 18:8; cf. {{Genesis 35:22|Gen 35:22}}; {{Genesis 49:4|49:4}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “(one who is) unclean due to the impurity they humble within you.” The use of the verb “to humble” suggests that these men forced themselves upon women during menstruation. Having sexual relations with a woman during her period was forbidden by the Law (Lev 18:19; 20:18).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “a man.”

*Translator's note:* The verb is the same one used in verse {{Ezekiel 22:10|10b}} and suggests forcible sexual violation of the woman.

*Study note:* Sexual relations with one’s half-sister may be primarily in view here. See Lev 18:9 and 20:17.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “usury and interest you take.” See {{Ezekiel 18:13|18:13}}, {{Ezekiel 18:17|17}}. This kind of economic exploitation violated the law given in Lev 25:36.

*Study note:* Forgetting the Lord is also addressed in {{Deuteronomy 6:12|Deut 6:12}}; {{Deuteronomy 8:11|8:11}}, {{Deuteronomy 8:14|14}}; Jer 3:21; 13:25; {{Ezekiel 23:35|Ezek 23:35}}; Hos 2:15; 8:14; 13:6.

*Translator's note:* The second person verb forms are feminine singular in Hebrew, indicating that the personified city is addressed here as representing its citizens.

*Study note:* This gesture apparently expresses mourning and/or anger (see {{Ezekiel 6:11|6:11}}; {{Ezekiel 21:14|21:14}}, {{Ezekiel 21:17|17}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the blood that was in you.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “stand.” The heart here stands for the emotions; Jerusalem would panic in the face of God’s judgment.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “in the days when I act against you.”
*Study note:* The ultimate purpose of divine judgment is to purify the covenant community of its sins.

*Translator's note:* The phrase “within yourself” is the same as the several previous occurrences of “within you” but adjusted to fit this clause, which is the culmination of the series of indictments.

*Text-critical note:* Several ancient versions read the verb as first person, in which case the Lord refers to how his people’s sin brings disgrace upon him. For a defense of the Hebrew text, see D. I. Block, *Ezekiel* (NICOT), 1:712, n. 68, and M. Greenberg, *Ezekiel* (AB), 2:457-58.
*Translator's note:* For similar imagery, see {{Isaiah 1:21|Isa 1:21-26}} and Jer 6:27-30.
*Translator's note:* The Hebrew second person pronoun is masculine plural here and in vv. {{Ezekiel 22:19|19b-21}}, indicating that the people are being addressed.
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “I will put.” No object is supplied in the Hebrew, prompting many to emend the text to “I will blow.” See *BHS* and verse {{Ezekiel 22:21|21}}.

*Text-critical note:* The MT reads: “that is not cleansed”; the LXX reads: “that is not drenched,” which assumes a different vowel pointing as well as the loss of a מ (mem) due to haplography. In light of the following reference to showers, the reading of the LXX certainly fits the context well. For a defense of the emendation, see L. C. Allen, *Ezekiel* (WBC), 2:32. Yet the MT is not an unreasonable reading since uncleanness in the land also fits the context. A poetic connection between rain and the land being uncleansed may be feasible since washing with water is elsewhere associated with cleansing ({{Numbers 8:7|Num 8:7}}; {{Numbers 31:23|31:23}}; {{Psalm 51:7|Ps 51:7}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “in a day of anger.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “a conspiracy of her prophets is in her midst.” The LXX reads “whose princes” rather than “a conspiracy of prophets.” The prophets are mentioned later in the paragraph (v. {{Ezekiel 22:28|28}}). If one follows the LXX in verse {{Ezekiel 22:25|25}}, then five distinct groups are mentioned in vv. {{Ezekiel 22:25|25-29}}: princes, priests, officials, prophets, and the people of the land. For a defense of the Septuagintal reading, see L. C. Allen, *Ezekiel* (WBC), 2:32, and D. I. Block, *Ezekiel* (NICOT), 1:720, n. 4.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “her widows they have multiplied.” The statement alludes to their murderous acts.

*Translator's note:* Or “between the consecrated and the common.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “hide their eyes from.” The idiom means to disregard or ignore something or someone (see Lev 20:4; {{1 Samuel 12:3|1 Sam 12:3}}; {{Proverbs 28:27|Prov 28:27}}; {{Isaiah 1:15|Isa 1:15}}).
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “Her prophets coat for themselves with whitewash.” The expression may be based on {{Ezekiel 13:10|Ezek 13:10-15}}.
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and the resident foreigner they have oppressed without justice.”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “their way on their head I have placed.”
*Translator's note:* In the Hebrew text the subject is left unstated and must be supplied from the context.

*Translator's note:* The names Oholah and Oholibah are both derived from the word meaning “tent.” The meaning of Oholah is “her tent,” while Oholibah means “my tent is in her.”

*Study note:* In this allegory the Lord is depicted as being the husband of two wives. The OT law prohibited a man from marrying sisters (Lev 18:18), but the practice is attested in the OT (cf. Jacob). The metaphor is utilized here for illustrative purposes and does not mean that the Lord condoned such a practice or bigamy in general.

*Study note:* *Engaged in prostitution* refers to alliances with pagan nations in this context. In {{Ezekiel 16|Ezek 16}} harlotry described the sin of idolatry.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “while she was under me.” The expression indicates that Oholah is viewed as the Lord’s wife. See {{Numbers 5:19|Num 5:19-20}}, {{Numbers 5:29|29}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “Assyria.”

*Translator's note:* The term apparently refers to Assyrian military officers; it is better construed with the description that follows. See D. I. Block, *Ezekiel* (NICOT), 1:738.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “lied down with.” The verb שָׁכַב (shakav) “to lie down” can imply going to bed to sleep or be a euphemism for sexual relations.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and poured out their harlotry on her.”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “I gave her into the hand of her lovers, into the hand of the sons of Assyria.”
*Translator's note:* The word “this” is not in the original text.
*Translator's note:* The only other occurrence of the Hebrew term is in Jer 22:14.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “at the appearance of her eyes.”

*Study note:* The Chaldeans were prominent tribal groups of Babylonia. The imagery is reminiscent of events in the reigns of Hezekiah ({{2 Kings 20:12|2 Kgs 20:12-15}}) and Jehoiakim ({{2 Kings 23:34|2 Kgs 23:34-24:1}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “The sons of Babel came to her on a bed of love.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “her soul.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “She exposed her harlotry and exposed her nakedness.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “my soul.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “my soul.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “She lusted after their concubines (?), whose flesh was the flesh of donkeys.” The phrase “their concubines” is difficult here. The pronoun is masculine plural, suggesting that the Egyptian men are in view, but how concubines would fit into the picture envisioned here is not clear. It is possible that the term refers here to the Egyptians’ genitals. The relative pronoun that follows introduces a more specific description of them. Some suggest that Ezekiel uses the term in an idiomatic sense of “paramour,” which is reflected in the translation above.

*Translator's note:* Or “you took note of.” The Hebrew verb פָּקַד (paqad) in the Qal implies evaluating something and then acting in light of that judgment; here the prophet depicts Judah as approving of her youthful unfaithfulness and then magnifying it at the present time. Some translations assume the verb should be repointed as a Niphal, rendering “you missed” or by extension “you longed for,” but such an extension of the Niphal “to be missing” is otherwise unattested.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “when (they) did,” but the verb makes no sense here and is better emended to “when (they) fondled,” a verb used in vv. {{Ezekiel 23:3|3}} and {{Ezekiel 23:8|8}}. See L. C. Allen, *Ezekiel* (WBC), 2:43.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “for the sake of,” but the expression is awkward and is better emended to read “to squeeze.” See L. C. Allen, *Ezekiel* (WBC), 2:43.
*Translator's note:* The word הִנֵּה (hinneh, traditionally “behold”) indicates becoming aware of something and has been translated here as a verb.

*Study note:* *Pekod* was the name of an Aramean tribe (known as Puqudu in Mesopotamian texts) that lived in the region of the Tigris River.

*Study note:* *Shoa* was the name of a nomadic people (the Sutu) that lived in Mesopotamia.

*Study note:* *Koa* was the name of another Mesopotamian people group (the Qutu).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “come against.”

*Translator's note:* This is the only occurrence of this term in the OT. The precise meaning is uncertain.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “an assembly of peoples.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “I will place before them judgment.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “give.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “they will remove.”

*Study note:* This method of punishment is attested among ancient Egyptian and Hittite civilizations. See W. Zimmerli, *Ezekiel* (Hermeneia), 1:489.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “fall.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “I will cause your obscene conduct to cease from you and your harlotry from the land of Egypt.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “lift your eyes to them.”

*Translator's note:* The word הִנֵּה (hinneh, traditionally “behold”) indicates becoming aware of something and has been translated here as a verb.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “I am giving you into the hand of.”

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew term means “labor,” but by extension it can also refer to that for which one works.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “The nakedness of your prostitution will be exposed, and your obscene conduct and your harlotry.”
*Translator's note:* The infinitive absolute continues the sequence begun in v. {{Ezekiel 23:28|28}}: “Look here, I am about to deliver you.” See Joüon 2:430 §123.w.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “her cup.” A cup of intoxicating strong drink is used, here and elsewhere, as a metaphor for judgment because both leave one confused and reeling. (See Jer 25:15, 17, 28; {{Habakkuk 2:16|Hab 2:16}}.) The cup of wrath is a theme also found in the NT ({{Mark 14:36|Mark 14:36}}).
*Study note:* The image of a deep and wide cup suggests the degree of punishment; it will be extensive and leave the victim helpless.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “You will drink it and drain (it).”

*Translator's note:* D. I. Block compares this to the idiom of “licking the plate” (*Ezekiel* [NICOT], 1:754, n. 137). The text is difficult as the word translated “gnaw” is rare. The noun is used of the shattered pieces of pottery and so could envision a broken cup. But the Piel verb form is used in only one other place ({{Numbers 24:8|Num 24:8}}), where it is a denominative from the noun “bone” and seems to mean to “break (bones).” Why it would be collocated with “sherds” is not clear. For this reason some emend the phrase to read “consume its dregs” (see L. C. Allen, *Ezekiel* [WBC], 2:44) or emend the verb to read “swallow,” as if the intoxicated Oholibah breaks the cup and then eats the very sherds in an effort to get every last drop of the beverage that dampens them.

*Study note:* The severe action is more extreme than beating the breasts in anguish ({{Isaiah 32:12|Isa 32:12}}; Nah 2:7). It is also ironic, for these are the very breasts she so blatantly offered to her lovers (vv. {{Ezekiel 23:3|3}}, {{Ezekiel 23:21|21}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and you cast me behind your back.” The expression pictures her rejection of the Lord (see {{1 Kings 14:9|1 Kgs 14:9}}).

*Translator's note:* As it stands in the MT, the syntax is difficult. Most translations say something like “groan in silence,” but this is problematic. According to their form, the two verbs that begin the verse, הֵאָנֵק (heʾanek; to groan) and דֹּם (dom; to be silent), may each be parsed as either imperative or infinitive construct. This allows four possible sequences. An infinitive followed by an infinitive would lack a main verb and can be dismissed. An infinitive followed by an imperative is improper syntax and nowhere occurs with both in the same clause. An imperative followed by an infinitive is very rare. The only three clear cases ({{Psalm 33:3|Ps 33:3}}; {{Isaiah 1:16|Isa 1:16}}; {{Isaiah 23:16|23:16}}) appear to involve infinitive complements, which does not fit these terms. Two imperatives back to back are common, occurring over 200 times, but in no case does the second imperative tell the manner of the action in the first (except perhaps a couple disputable parsings of מַהֵר (maher; be quick). So there is no combination of the forms in the MT that supports the common translation. It may also be said that groaning and being silent are mutually exclusive concepts. However, there is a rare homonym, also attested in the cognate languages Ugaritic and Akkadian, another root דמם (dmm), which means to moan. The translation above follows the suggestion of M. Greenberg that דֹּם מֵתִים (dom metim) be taken together and דֹּם be derived from דָּמַם (damam, “to moan, murmur”) meaning: “Groan a moaning for the dead.” See M. Greenberg, *Ezekiel* (AB), 2:508. Note that in verse {{Ezekiel 24:23|23}} Ezekiel affirms that the people will moan to each other (though there the root is נָהַם, naham); therefore, it is reasonable to suppose that Ezekiel is moaning here, since his actions forecast theirs.

The presence of a conjunction at the beginning of “I placed you” is problematic for the proposal, but it may reflect a later misunderstanding of the syntax of the verse. It also refers to large creatures that inhabit the sea ({{Genesis 1:21|Gen 1:21}}; {{Psalm 148:7|Ps 148:7}}). In several passages it is associated with the sea or with the multiheaded sea monster Leviathan ({{Job 7:12|Job 7:12}}; {{Psalm 74:13|Ps 74:13}}; {{Isaiah 27:1|Isa 27:1}}; {{Isaiah 51:9|51:9}}). Because of the Egyptian setting of this prophecy and the reference to the creature’s scales (v. {{Ezekiel 29:4|4}}), many understand a crocodile to be the referent here (e.g., NCV “a great crocodile”; TEV “you monster crocodile”; CEV “a giant crocodile”).
